html:
The moa, giant flightless birds found only in New Zealand, were hunted to extinction within about two centuries after people arrived, by around 1400. There were nine species. The largest stood about 3.6 metres tall with neck stretched and weighed over 200 kg; the smallest was the size of a turkey.

Moa had no land predators except the huge Haast's eagle, so they did not fear the Polynesian settlers who came in the late 1200s; see Māori settle Aotearoa. Early sites such as Wairau Bar are full of moa bones, butchered meat and eggshell, and moa bone was used for fish hooks and ornaments. The birds bred slowly, and a small human population with dogs, fire and forest clearing was enough to wipe them out. Haast's eagle died with them.

It is one of the clearest cases of people causing an extinction, a smaller and faster version of what happened to large animals elsewhere; see Quaternary extinction event. With moa gone, Māori turned to fish, birds, fern root and kūmara, and built fortified villages as competition for land grew.
